prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay on whether it is wrong to eat animals
raw:
I remember the exact weight of the knife—187 grams, a Wüsthof Classic, the one with the full tang and the black synthetic handle. I was standing in a rented farmhouse kitchen in the Drôme, and the rabbit on the counter was still faintly warm. Not warm from the sun but from a life that had ended eight minutes earlier. It had a name, which was ridiculous. My neighbor, a man named Lucien who had the knuckles of a stonemason and a sad, magnificent dog named Balthazar, had named the rabbit Noisette because of the hazel coloring around its left eye. Lucien killed it by holding its back legs in his left hand, placing a thumb just behind its ears, and pulling with a swift upward motion until he felt the vertebrae separate. There was no scream. The scream, I’ve learned, is what humans imagine an animal *should* do. The rabbit simply left the world in a shudder, a jerk, and then a stillness so complete it felt reproachful.

Was it wrong? I think the question is misfiled in our moral library. We want to put it under Ethics, where it rubs elbows with Kant and Mill, but it really belongs in the untidy section marked Tragedy, or perhaps Love. Any honest inquiry into whether it is wrong to eat animals must start not with the animal, but with the eater. And I am an eater, specifically, a lifelong carnivore who has also, and this is the part that makes my vegetarian friends flinch, killed the things I’ve eaten. Not many. A few rabbits, a couple of wild ducks, one deeply regrettable rooster who attacked my ankle and whom I dispatched in a fury that I later had to process as murder. I have seen the inside of a small slaughterhouse in Gascony where the ducks stand on a steel grate, their necks threaded into a metal cone, the blood draining into a trench that smells of iron and wet feathers. I have plucked a woodcock while its breast was still hot, my thumb slipping into the cavity beneath the keel bone to scoop out the heart, which I ate raw, still pulpy, with flecks of salt. I am not neutral on this subject.

The prevailing case against meat-eating leans heavily on the capacity for suffering. Peter Singer, from his utilitarian citadel, gave us the moral slide rule: if a being can suffer, its suffering matters. The calculus is clean, the conclusion as sharp as a guillotine. Commercial meat is an unending atrocity of debeaking, gestation crates, and the existential horror of a broiler chicken that lives its entire forty-seven days under a roof it will never understand as anything other than a dim, ammoniac universe of pain. I have walked through an industrial pig barn in North Carolina where the sows are immobilized in farrowing crates, their piglets scurrying over a slatted floor that separates them from the concrete pit of waste below. A worker showed me how to dock a piglet’s tail with a pair of side-cutting pliers. No anesthetic. The sound is a wet pop and a squeal that modulates into a frequency I still carry in my tinnitus. If sheer tonnage of suffering were the only metric, I would have to conclude that consuming any animal product from that system is not merely wrong but a form of profound moral cowardice. And I do conclude that. I haven’t eaten factory-farmed pork in eighteen years.

But the argument takes a strange turn when it leaps from that charnel house to the sunlit pasture where Lucien kept his rabbits. Singer’s logic makes a radically democratic move—all suffering is equal, a nervy proposition that flattens the world into an undifferentiated smear of nerve endings. Yet I know, not in the abstract but in the hands and gut, that killing Noisette was a different category of event. The rabbit had a life worth a rabbit’s living: sweet alfalfa, the company of other rabbits, the smell of September grass, a death delivered faster than any predator could manage. This is not a clean moral transaction. It is, instead, an old, uneasy covenant. You take a life you cannot give back, and you do it with the full knowledge of what you are doing. The wrongness, and there *is* a wrongness, is precisely the point. It should stick in your throat. The day it doesn’t, you have become a machine.

I believe, contra the mainstream vegetarian argument, that the moral weight of eating an animal is not a bug but a feature. It is a way of staying tethered to the bloody, difficult reality of being one creature among many, all of us converting life into life. The great failure of industrial meat is not that it kills—every meal kills something, including the soy harvest that minces field mice and baby rabbits in the combine blades—but that it makes killing abstract. It transforms an animal into a unit, a “finished steer” with a target weight of 1,350 pounds, its flesh graded on a marbling score from 1 to 12. I have used a camera to peer into the digestive tract of a live steer through a fistula, a permanent hole in its side, in an experiment at the University of California, Davis. The steer, number 831, stood placidly while a graduate student fished out a bolus of half-digested alfalfa. That steer was a research tool. It was also a steer. It would end up at a processor in Imperial County, and its meat would be sold to a campus dining hall. I found that impossible to parse, and I still do.

Perhaps the deepest, least comfortable truth is that the wrongness of eating animals is a function of attention. If you have held the dying weight, if you have felt the way a jackrabbit’s legs continue to paddle after the head is off, you cannot pretend you are an innocent consumer of protein. You are implicated. But implication, I think, is the correct posture for a human being. We are all implicated in the deaths that sustain us, whether they are the deaths of chickens or the deaths of the migrant workers who pick our kale. The fantasy of a clean, murder-free diet is exactly that—a fantasy. The question is not whether we kill, but whether we are willing to live with the killing we do, to know the heft of the knife and the name of the animal and the particular shudder of a life leaving a body. That does not excuse the factory farm; it indicts it even more harshly, because the factory farm robs us of even the possibility of that burdened, sacred attention.

So no, I don’t think it is wrong to eat animals. I think it is wrong to eat them carelessly. I think eating an animal is a form of inheritance, a participation in an old, violent, tender ecology that we are close to forgetting. The last duck I shot was on a saltmarsh in Brittany. It was a Eurasian wigeon, a drake in full plumage. I shot it at thirty yards with a 12-gauge, and it folded and fell into the cordgrass. When I picked it up, the eye was still bright. I whispered something—an apology, a thank you—and I meant it. Then I brought it home, plucked it, roasted it with thyme and a split garlic clove, and sat down with my wife to eat it. The meal was quiet. The duck was delicious. And I still carry the small, permanent knot of that day in my chest, which is the whole terrible and necessary arrangement.
